planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in a sunny, sheltered spot in well-drained soil; where winters drop below the high teens F, grow it in a pot that can be moved under cover.

directions: Miles Choice is a selection of common bay laurel bred for a denser, more upright habit than the species, with smaller, more crowded glossy dark-green leaves that make it especially forgiving of regular shearing. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and let the top few inches dry between waterings once established. Because it holds a tidy shape with less pruning effort than seed-grown bay, it is favored for clipped hedges, screens, and formal standards, though the aromatic leaves can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like ordinary bay laurel. In marginal zones grow it in a container and shelter it from hard freezes and drying winter wind.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Laurus nobilis

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown stock in spring in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; this slow, naturally small cultivar suits patio pots and rarely needs repotting into anything large.

directions: Bay Junior is a naturally dwarf, slow-growing bay laurel cultivar with smaller, more delicate leaves than the species, bred for patio and container culture rather than for eventual tree size. It tolerates colder winters better than plain bay laurel and needs only a light annual trim to keep its neat, rounded head. Grow it in well-drained soil in a sunny, sheltered position, or in a pot that can be brought into an unheated porch or garage during severe cold. The small aromatic leaves can be picked and used fresh or dried exactly like standard bay leaf, though a mature plant yields a modest harvest given its diminutive size.
sources: Shoot Gardening plant database — Laurus nobilis 'Bay Junior'

subcategory: dwarf ball-form culinary bay laurel cultivar

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; this plant-breeders'-rights selection naturally forms a dense ball and needs only occasional light shaping to keep that outline.

directions: Baby Bay is a plant-breeders'-rights-protected selection of common bay laurel valued for its naturally rounded, dense growth habit, which holds a neat ball or standard shape with far less clipping than seed-grown bay requires. Its small, glossy, aromatic leaves are used in cooking exactly like ordinary bay laurel, making it a dual-purpose choice for growers who also want a tidy topiary specimen. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil and let it dry out somewhat between waterings, since it dislikes wet feet. In cold climates keep it as a container plant and move it to a sheltered spot before hard frost arrives.
sources: IP Australia Plant Breeder's Rights database — Laurus nobilis 'Baby Bay'

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out nursery divisions in spring into well-drained, even sandy or poor soil in full sun; this short-lived perennial relative of common borage is hardier and more drought-tolerant than annual borage but still benefits from good drainage.

directions: Creeping borage is a low, sprawling perennial relative of common borage, native to Corsica, Sardinia, and the nearby island of Capraia, forming loose rosettes of hairy, oval leaves topped by airy sprays of pale blue, bell-shaped flowers from late spring into autumn. Unlike annual borage it persists for a few seasons as a woody-based perennial and tolerates dry, lean, gravelly ground better than its taprooted cousin. Grow it in full sun in sharply drained soil, where it works well as a front-of-border filler, in dry gravel gardens, or trailing over a low wall. The edible flowers can be used as a cucumber-flavored garnish just as with common borage, and the plant self-sows lightly in favorable spots without becoming aggressive.
sources: Jekka's Herb Farm — Borago pygmaea (Prostrate Borage)
BBC Gardeners' World Magazine — Borago pygmaea

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes in average, well-drained soil in full sun; like other borage strains it resents transplanting once the taproot forms, and seedlings that emerge with plain green leaves should be thinned out to keep the patch variegated.

directions: Variegata is an RHS-recognized variegated strain of common borage in which the coarse, hairy green leaves carry an irregular white mottling and marbling across the leaf surface, distinct from the bolder cream-splashed blotches of the 'Bill Archer' strain. It otherwise grows and flowers like ordinary borage, producing the same brilliant blue, star-shaped blooms on a bristly annual plant. Direct sow where it is to grow, since the taproot is easily damaged, and remove any all-green seedlings early to keep the planting showy. Harvest the young leaves and flowers for the same mild, cucumber-like flavor prized in the species, and allow a few plants to self-sow if a repeat patch is wanted the following year.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Borago officinalis
